decisions.summary: Two independent accounts—an official council-minutes record compiled from roll call and an attending reporter's own tally—both state the bridge plan passed seven to two on 1 June 2024, with no recorded reversal.

evidence.finding: Council minutes for the 1 June 2024 meeting record approval of the bridge plan with seven votes for and two against, compiled by the clerk from the recorded roll call.
An attending reporter independently tallied the roll call and confirms the plan passed seven to two on 1 June 2024, reporting no subsequent reversal at that meeting.

decisions.summary: Both a contemporaneous interview transcript and an independent audio recording by Reporter B confirm Mayor Imani made the stated statement on 2024-02-02.

evidence.finding: Transcript dated 2024-02-02 records Mayor Imani saying Eastport unemployment fell by 20 percent between 2022 and 2023.
Reporter B's independent audio recording of the same 2024-02-02 interview contains Mayor Imani saying the 20 percent figure.

gaps: The embedded statistic itself is not verified and is addressed under the separate insufficient_content case.

decisions.summary: The only records corroborate that Mayor Imani stated the 20 percent decline, but the statement's embedded statistic is unverified—no unemployment dataset, methodology, or independent measurement is supplied.

evidence.finding: Records show only Mayor Imani's spoken assertion, with each record explicitly noting that no dataset is provided and the statistic was not verified.
Reporter B independently confirms the quote but explicitly did not verify the statistic.

gaps: No unemployment data or methodology for 2022–2023 Eastport supplied.
Base population and definition of the 20 percent change unspecified.

decisions.summary: Lab A's independent citywide 2023 sample yields a 28-minute median supporting the claim while Lab B's independent, non-overlapping sample yields 34 minutes refuting it, and the discrepancy is explicitly unresolved.

evidence.finding: Lab A's independent 2023 citywide sample (order-confirmed to door-received) estimates a 28-minute median, under 30.
Lab B's independent 2023 citywide sample, computed without Lab A's observations or calculations, estimates a 34-minute median, over 30; the discrepancy is unresolved.

gaps: Sampling or methodological cause of the 28 vs 34 minute discrepancy unidentified in the supplied records.
contradictions: W1 (28 min) vs W2 (34 min) directly disagree on the same population, metric, and period.

decisions.summary: The causal 15 percent claim originates solely from the vendor's press release, which admits no adjustment for traffic volume, construction, or seasonality, and the Bulletin merely repeats it without independent verification.

evidence.finding: Vendor press release asserts the 15 percent reduction was caused by the signal system, comparing before/after observations without adjusting for traffic volume, construction, seasonality, or other changes.
Southport Bulletin repeats the vendor's figures and explicitly did not collect or independently verify any measurements, so it adds no independent support for the causal claim.

gaps: No analysis isolating the signal system's causal effect from traffic volume, construction, seasonality, or other confounders.
No independent measurement of delays exists among the supplied records.

decisions.summary: A calculation based on Federal Reserve SCF data finds Bloomberg's $64.2B net worth exceeds the combined ~$11.4B wealth of the bottom 38 percent of households (~125.7 million people), and an independent replication found the comparison holds even though it estimated a lower bottom-38% figure of $6 billion.

evidence.finding: Peoples Policy Project (Bruenig) calculation: Bloomberg's $64.2B (per Forbes) vs bottom 38% of households (~47.8M households × 2.63 members ≈ 125.7M people) with collective net worth of $11.4B per SCF, i.e., Bloomberg owns nearly six times as much—so he owns more than the bottom 125 million Americans combined.

PolitiFact had an independent analyst replicate Bruenig's math; the analyst found the bottom 38% held about $6 billion (lower than $11.4B), and concluded this verified that Bloomberg had more wealth than the bottom 38% of households combined.
Jacobin states the same Bloomberg ($64.2B) vs bottom 38% ($11.4B SCF) comparison, but the figures and framing match S1's calculation, indicating shared origin rather than independent corroboration.

S4 (Common Dreams) and S5 (snippets) only report that Sanders stated the claim at the debate; they repeat, not verify, the statistic, and S6/S7 snippets concern different wealth comparisons outside this claim's scope.

gaps: Underlying 2019 SCF microdata and Forbes net-worth basis are not directly supplied; verification rests on the S1 calculation and the S2 replication report.
Replication's $6B vs original $11.4B divergence for the bottom 38% is noted but the cause of the discrepancy is not resolved in the supplied records (does not change the conclusion either way).
contradictions: S2's replicated bottom-38% wealth ($6B) differs numerically from S1/S3's figure ($11.4B), though both values support the claim as worded.
